analysis.one_liner: Requires health insurance to cover prescription contraception, expands family planning funding, and writes the Roe v. Wade standard into federal law.
analysis.headline: Introduced in September 1997 with 50 cosponsors, the bill was sent to three House committees and died there without ever getting a vote before the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required employer health plans and insurers to cover prescription contraceptives on the same terms as other prescription drugs, authorized $275 million a year for family planning programs, funded public education about emergency contraception, and made it federal law that states cannot restrict abortion before fetal viability — the standard the Supreme Court set in Roe v. Wade. It also would have restored abortion coverage in military health care for cases of rape, incest, or medical necessity, and blocked federal 'gag rule' restrictions on clinics sharing reproductive health information. The bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote in any committee or chamber.
analysis.who_benefits: Women of childbearing age, who would no longer pay out of pocket for contraceptives that most insurance plans excluded (the bill's findings note women of reproductive age spend 68% more than men out of pocket); low-income women on Medicaid, whose access to abortion funding the bill endorsed; military women and dependents overseas, who would regain abortion access in cases of rape, incest, or medical need; and family planning clinics, which would receive funding and federal protection from violence and harassment.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Women, especially low-income and military women

how_it_helps.text: Bars group health plans and insurers from excluding or restricting coverage of FDA-approved prescription contraceptives and outpatient contraceptive services if the plan covers other prescription drugs or outpatient services, in both the group and individual markets [S3].
Prohibits plans from denying enrollment, paying people to accept less protection, or rewarding health professionals for steering patients away from contraception [S3].

Authorizes $275 million for fiscal year 1999 for voluntary family planning grants, citing the finding that every $1 of public family planning money saves $4 to $14 in pregnancy and health care costs [S3].

Requires a public education program on emergency contraception and directs the government to let the FDA's decision on the abortion pill RU-486 be made on the ordinary legal basis, plus assess promoting U.S. manufacturing of the drug [S2, S3].
Establishes as a matter of federal statute the Roe v. Wade rule: states may not restrict abortion before fetal viability, and only within limits after viability [S3].
Restores Department of Defense funding for abortions in cases of rape, incest, or medical necessity and allows abortions at military facilities overseas when paid with non-Defense funds [S2].
Adds a federal prohibition on any government program limiting the right to give or receive nonfraudulent information about reproductive health services, blocking 'gag rule' policies [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers and health insurers would bear the cost of the new contraceptive coverage mandate, likely passed partly into premiums; taxpayers would fund the family planning grants, emergency contraception education, and any restored military abortion coverage. Opponents of abortion also objected to codifying the Roe v. Wade standard and to federal abortion funding for Medicaid-eligible women.

drawbacks.text: The contraceptive coverage mandate raises costs for employers and insurers offering prescription drug benefits; the bill allows cost-sharing but caps it at the level charged for other drugs, meaning plans cannot shift the added cost onto contraceptive users alone [S3].
The $275 million family planning authorization plus a $5 million emergency contraception education program would be new federal spending [S3].

The bill codifies the Roe v. Wade standard as statutory law and endorses Medicaid funding of abortion services — provisions that millions of Americans who oppose abortion reject on principle, and that opponents argued exceed Congress's proper role [S3].
The federal mandate would override state decisions not to require contraceptive coverage in insurance, preempting state policy choices except where states offer stronger protections [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core insurance provision directly addresses a documented gap — most plans covered other prescription drugs but excluded contraceptives, leaving women paying hundreds of dollars a year out of pocket — and the bill's own findings link that gap to roughly 3 million unintended pregnancies annually. The costs are real but modest and standard for a benefit mandate. The abortion-related titles (codifying Roe, Medicaid abortion funding, military coverage) are the provisions that made the bill politically heavy, and they are what gave opponents reason to bury it; a narrower contraception-equity bill might have fared better.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to three House committees on the day it was introduced and then to three subcommittees, and none of them ever reported it out — so it sat until the 105th Congress ended in January 1999 with no hearing, no markup, and no vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Nita Lowey introduced the bill on September 23, 1997, joined by 10 original cosponsors including Reps. Pelosi, Norton, Maloney, and DeLauro [S3].
It drew 49 additional cosponsors — 47 Democrats, 1 Independent, and 1 Republican [S4].

The Speaker referred it to three committees at once: Commerce, Judiciary, and Education and the Workforce, a multiple referral that requires each committee to act on provisions in its jurisdiction [S5].

Over the following weeks it was sent to subcommittees — the Constitution Subcommittee (Judiciary) on September 26, Employer-Employee Relations (Education and the Workforce) on October 3, and Health and Environment (Commerce) on October 15 — and no further action was ever recorded [S5].
No committee reported the bill, and it never reached the House floor before the Congress ended on January 3, 1999 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, employers and insurers never had to cover prescription contraceptives, no family planning money was authorized, and opponents of codified abortion rights kept the status quo — while the women the bill was written for gained nothing.

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly Democratic — 47 of 49 cosponsors — with one Republican and one Independent joining; no vote ever occurred, so no roll-call split exists, and the bill died in committees chaired by Republicans.

industries.note: The bill would bar insurers from excluding contraceptives from prescription drug coverage in the group and individual markets, adding a mandated benefit insurers had widely excluded — the bill's findings found only 7% of HMOs covered any contraceptive method besides sterilization. The cost of the mandate lands on insurers and the premiums they charge.

ERISA group plans would have to cover prescription contraceptives on equal terms with other drugs, a new benefit cost for employers. The bill caps cost-sharing for contraceptives at the level charged for other drugs, so plans could not recover the added cost from contraceptive users alone.

Mandated coverage across group and individual markets would expand the market for FDA-approved contraceptive drugs and devices, and the bill directs federal promotion of U.S. testing and manufacturing of RU-486 and other antiprogestins.

industries.industry: Family planning clinics and abortion providers
industries.note: The bill authorizes $275 million in family planning grants, declares federal resources should combat clinic violence and harassment, and bars government gag rules on reproductive health information — directly supporting clinic operations and safety.
